questions.stem: Andre, 65, has CT-confirmed acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. The report shows no discrete mass but says an underlying neoplasm cannot be excluded in the thickened segment. A colleague of his recently had bowel cancer. He asks you, 'Is it cancer, Doc?' Which response best answers him?
options: No, the CT was clear, so cancer is ruled out and you won't need any more tests
We'll do a colonoscopy tomorrow while you're in hospital so we can check properly
No sign of it on the scan, but swelling can hide one, so a camera test in about 6 weeks
Restart the bowel screening poo test after you go home and we'll go from there
questions.why: CT cannot exclude cancer in an inflamed, thickened segment. Arrange a colonoscopy (or CT colonography) about 6 weeks after recovery, and tell him honestly that this is the plan.
notes: This gives false reassurance: wall thickening can hide a tumour, so luminal assessment is still needed after the episode.
Colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis is contraindicated because insufflation can perforate the inflamed bowel.
A faecal occult blood test is a screening tool for people without symptoms and does not replace direct imaging of the lumen in a man with a thickened sigmoid segment.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, is on day 3 of IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole for CT-confirmed uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. He is still febrile at 38.4 °C, his LIF pain is no better and his CRP has risen from 128 to 190. He is haemodynamically stable and the tenderness is still localised. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent colonoscopy to look directly at the inflamed sigmoid segment
Repeat CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to look for an abscess
Emergency laparotomy and Hartmann's procedure today
Switch to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and plan discharge
questions.why: If diverticulitis is not improving after 48 to 72 hours of treatment, repeat the CT to look for a complication such as a pericolic or pelvic abscess. An abscess may need percutaneous drainage.
notes: Colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute diverticulitis because of the risk of perforation, and it would not show an extraluminal collection.
Emergency surgery is for perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis or for uncontrolled sepsis. A stable patient with localised signs needs imaging first.
Fever and a rising CRP mean he is not responding. Stepping down to oral antibiotics and discharging him would miss a developing complication.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, eats a low-fibre diet ('meat and three veg, white bread'). His CT shows multiple diverticula in the sigmoid and distal descending colon, one of which is now inflamed. Which mechanism best explains how these diverticula formed?
options: High segmental pressure pushes mucosa and submucosa through vasa recta entry points
Congenital weakness produces outpouchings that include every layer of the colonic wall
Inferior mesenteric artery ischaemia thins the wall so it balloons outward
Chronic mucosal inflammation from bile acids erodes through the muscularis propria
questions.why: Colonic diverticula are pulsion pseudodiverticula. High intraluminal pressure, which is greatest in the narrow sigmoid and made worse by low-fibre stool, pushes mucosa and submucosa through gaps in the circular muscle where the vasa recta penetrate.
notes: That describes a true diverticulum, such as Meckel's. Colonic diverticula are acquired and contain no muscle layer.
Ischaemia causes ischaemic colitis, not diverticula. The vessels matter only because the points where they enter the wall are weak.
Diverticula form through mechanical herniation, not erosion from inflammation. Inflammation comes later, as diverticulitis.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, has sigmoid diverticulitis. His pain is now constant and sharply localised to the left iliac fossa, worse with coughing and with every bump in the car, and he has rebound tenderness there. Early colonic pain is usually vague and felt in the midline. Which nerves carry this localised pain?
options: Visceral afferents running with sympathetic fibres to the L1 to L2 cord segments
Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) carrying afferents from the sigmoid wall
Genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2) irritated where it runs on psoas major
Somatic nerves of the parietal peritoneum, from lower thoracic and L1 spinal nerves
questions.why: Once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, pain travels in the somatic nerves that supply the overlying abdominal wall (lower intercostal, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal). That is why it is sharply localised and made worse by movement.
notes: Hindgut visceral afferents give poorly localised, dull pain referred to the hypogastrium, not sharp LIF pain with rebound.
Pelvic splanchnic afferents are visceral too. They carry stretch and pain from the distal colon that is poorly localised.
Genitofemoral irritation would cause pain in the groin or thigh. The psoas sign tests for retroperitoneal inflammation, not localised LIF peritonism.
